column4: Hell itself is called مِرْصَادًا, the same road-watchpoint named by the section; the next ayah identifies the transgressors for whom it waits.
The exact summons أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ makes the hearer witness what the Lord did to the elephant army, just as 89:6 does with ʿĀd.
Iblis vows to sit for human beings on God's straight path; this is the section's stationary watcher waiting where every traveler must go.
Shuʿayb forbids his people to sit threatening on every path and bar believers, a human enactment of the road turned into an ambush point.
The order to sit for treaty-breakers at كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍ uses the ر ص د place-word for an actual set of waiting positions on their routes.
A jinn seeking a listening-place now finds a flame شِهَابًا رَصَدًا waiting for him, matching the traveler who discovers the watcher only when struck.
God places رَصَدًا before and behind an approved messenger; the same root depicts watchers stationed along a person's route rather than pursuing him.
Every utterance finds beside the speaker a ready watcher, رَقِيبٌ عَتِيدٌ, directly extending the section's watching eye to speech.
At judgment the person's covering is removed and sight becomes sharp; this realizes the section's inward eye only when the concealed watch has reached its outcome.
The declaration that the human being transgresses joins the section's ٱلْإِنسَانُ to its sense of طغيان as crossing the limit.
The human transgresses because he رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, sees himself self-sufficient; this is precisely the inward gaze that mistakes abundance for honor.
أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ corrects the self-regarding person's view with the divine gaze that has watched throughout.
ʿĀd see the approaching cloud and read it as rain, although it is the punishment they hastened; their visual misreading concretely parallels the human's two false readings of one test.
The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command until only dwellings can be seen, supplying the visible aftermath that the hearer of 89:6 is told to behold; 46:24 names the fatal misreading.
ʿĀd's hearing, eyes, and hearts avail them nothing despite their endowment, directly testing the section's distinction between possessing eyes and seeing with insight.
Travel through the land should produce hearts that reason and ears that hear, for it is hearts rather than eyes that go blind; this unites the section's travelers, ruins, and inward sight.
The dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamūd remain apparent, yet Satan barred them from the path although they were مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ; visible ruins, blocked road, and failed insight meet in one ayah.
ٱلْإِنسَانُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِۦ بَصِيرَةٌ makes the human being an inward witness against himself, the Quranic counterpart to the section's figure seen within the eye.
If provision were expanded without measure people would transgress, so God sends it in due measure and remains seeing of His servants; provision, limit-crossing, measure, and the watcher coincide.
God expands and restricts provision while being fully aware and seeing of His servants, correcting the human who treats those two measures as honor and humiliation.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا۟ introduces the same fact that God expands and restricts provision, making right seeing the cure for the section's mistaken twofold judgment.
Those who had wished for Qārūn's place now recognize that God expands and restricts provision; the sight of his collapse in 28:81 corrects their former reading of wealth.
طَغَا ٱلْمَآءُ uses ط غ ي for water crossing its bound rather than rebellion, while the ark passes through the divinely controlled catastrophe.
The rescue is made a reminder retained by a receptive ear; after 69:5-11 display the old peoples and the overflowing water, perception must turn the scene into a lesson.
The hearer is ordered to return the gaze over creation and ask whether any fissure can be seen, beginning the deliberate repeated looking opposed to a distorted self-view.
The command to return sight كَرَّتَيْنِ gives the section's “eye looking two looks” a disciplined counterpart: repeated sight returns humbled and exhausted, not doubled into false judgments.
أَلَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُۥ عَيْنَيْنِ grounds the section's doubled-eye wordplay in the two eyes actually granted to the human being and for which he is accountable.
Every one of the addressed people will come to Hell by an irrevocable decree, closely matching the watchpoint placed on a route every traveler must meet.
The wrongdoers are directed to صِرَٰطِ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, turning the road itself toward Hell; 37:24 supplies the halt on that road.
“Stop them; they are to be questioned” stages the unavoidable checkpoint at the end of the path named in 37:23.
Thamūd's conspirators swear to make a night attack on Ṣāliḥ and his family, setting up human watchers who believe they control the unseen strike.
They plot while God counters their plot without their perceiving it, reversing the apparent watcher and the true watcher before the blow in 27:51.
The hearer is told to look at the plotters' outcome: they and their people are destroyed, making the hidden counter-watch visible only in its result.
The addressees have passed repeatedly by the town rained upon with evil rain, yet failed to see it; travelers literally cross a punishment-site without gaining the inward lesson.
The Meccans pass the destroyed people of Lot in the morning, making the old judgment a site on their ordinary route.
They also pass it by night and are asked whether they will reason; the ayah joins night travel to the failure to read what the eye sees.
The destroyed towns contain signs for careful observers, ٱلْمُتَوَسِّمِينَ, naming the discriminating gaze the section asks of its listener.
The ruins lie on an enduring, established road, so the lesson in 15:75 is literally waiting where travelers pass.
Moses is commanded to take the servants by night and strike a dry path through the sea without fear of being overtaken, combining night travel, a necessary route, and a waiting pursuer.
Pharaoh follows them onto that path and the sea overwhelms him, revealing the route itself as the place where the transgressor is caught.
Lot is told to travel with his household during part of the night, not turn back, and trust a morning appointment; gaze, night route, and an inescapable descending judgment meet.
Lot is commanded to set out in a portion of the night, follow behind his people, forbid backward looks, and proceed where ordered, an exact night-traveler scene disciplined by sight.
God tells Moses to take His servants by night because they will be pursued, placing the traveling group and its would-be catcher on the same route.
The command to take God's servants by night because they will be followed repeats the section's س ر ي sense and leads the pursuers into the sea's blow.
God is not unaware of what wrongdoers do; He only delays them to a day when eyes stare, expressing the watcher who waits rather than immediately chasing.
On that delayed day they rush forward with heads raised and gaze unable to return, making the watched travelers' own eyes part of the judgment announced in 14:42.
Moses is sent to Pharaoh because إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ, the same limit-crossing in rebellion exemplified by the Pharaoh observed in the section.
God seizes Pharaoh with an exemplary punishment for his latter and former claim, giving the delayed watcher’s decisive blow.
The seizure in 79:25 is explicitly an عِبْرَةً for one who fears, realizing the source dictionary's “parable as a lesson seen.”
When Pharaoh's people provoke divine anger, God takes vengeance and drowns them all, the same observed divine action against a land-transgressor.
Their destruction makes them a precedent and مَثَلًا for later people; the section's م ث ل branch as lesson is stated directly after the blow.
The hearers are told to take lesson, O people of sight, after God reaches a fortified people from where they did not expect; hidden watching becomes visible outcome.
God's alternation of night and day contains an عِبْرَةً for people of sight, joining the passing night to perceptive seeing rather than mere eyesight.
The statement that guardians stand over human beings makes the section's watcher a continuous presence over every traveler.
The guardians are noble recorders, specifying the kind of observer introduced in 82:10.
They know whatever people do, completing the stationary watch whose evidence appears when judgment arrives.
Every soul has a guardian over it, a concise universal form of the section's inescapable watching position.
God knows the stealthy betrayal of eyes and what breasts conceal, uniting the outer eye, the inner condition, and the watcher neither can evade.
Good and evil alike are tests before return to God, directly correcting the division of one trial into “honor” and “humiliation.”
The scattered people are tested with good things and bad things so that they may return, another explicit single testing purpose behind opposite conditions.
The question asks whether wealth and sons are being read as God hastening good to their owners, exactly exposing the section's prosperity-equals-honor inference.
بَل لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ denies that inference as a failure of perception, completing the question in 23:55.
God expands and restricts provision, though most people do not know; the two economic states therefore cannot bear the two judgments the human assigns them.
Wealth and children do not bring anyone nearer to God, explicitly severing abundance from the honor presumed in 34:35-36.
After harm, a human receives favor and says it came by his own knowledge; God calls it a test, exposing the inward gaze that misreads a changed condition.
Solomon sees the throne settled before him and names the favor a test of gratitude rather than proof of personal honor.
After adversity, a person tastes mercy and says “this is mine” while dismissing the Hour, a direct instance of favor distorted by self-regard.
God first touches the people of towns with hardship and adversity so that they may humble themselves, establishing deprivation as purposeful testing rather than humiliation.
Adversity is exchanged for prosperity, but their misreading is followed by a sudden seizure; the same two conditions culminate at the unseen watchpoint.
After people forget the warning, every gate of prosperity is opened; while they exult, they are seized suddenly, showing bounty immediately before the waiting blow.
Those distracted by competitive abundance will surely see Hell, shifting sight from the wealth they counted to the watchpoint they ignored.
They will see it with the eye of certainty, the final sharpened gaze following 102:6's disclosure of Hell.
The person thought he would never return, yet his Lord was always seeing him; the ayah corrects 84:14's self-reading by disclosing the patient watcher.
Boiling water is poured مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمْ, making the section's ص ب ب movement an explicit punishment descending from above.
The keepers are ordered to pour the punishment of boiling water over the sinner's head, another literal punitive ص ب ب from above.
ʿĀd are destroyed by a furious wind, placing the very people shown in 89:6 before the reader in another visible punishment scene.
The wind is imposed for seven nights and eight days so the people lie like hollow palm trunks, displaying the prolonged blow named in 69:6.
فَهَلْ تَرَىٰ لَهُم مِّنۢ بَاقِيَةٍ turns ʿĀd's disappearance into a direct question to the observer's eye.
Thamūd insolently cross their Lord's command and are seized by the thunderbolt while looking, bringing transgression, blow, and the victim's gaze together.
Thamūd deny in their طَغْوَىٰ, attaching the section's limit-crossing word directly to one of its observed peoples.
After hamstringing the camel, their Lord crushes and levels them for their sin, the decisive consequence of the transgression named in 91:11.
The singular command to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed,” frames the same transgressor as the object of a divine mission before his capture.
Moses and Aaron together receive the command to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, repeating the stance with two witnesses sent to the limit-crosser.
The one who طَغَىٰ is classified by the same act of exceeding the limit that characterizes the old peoples.
Preferring the nearer life supplies the inward valuation behind the transgression in 79:37.
Hell becomes that person's refuge, completing the transgressor-to-watchpoint sequence also stated in 78:21-22.
Qārūn, Pharaoh, and Hāmān act arrogantly in the land but cannot outrun God, answering the section's country-crossers with a limit no traveler can pass.
Each people is seized for its sin by a distinct calamity, including a stone-storm and earth swallowing, making the unseen watch visible as precisely fitted blows.
Thamūd prefer blindness over guidance, then the thunderbolt seizes them; failed inner sight and the observed blow form one causal scene.
The audience dwells in the homes of wrongdoers, has been shown how God dealt with them, and has received examples; route, sight, divine action, and م ث ل-as-lesson converge.
مَا زَاغَ ٱلْبَصَرُ وَمَا طَغَىٰ describes sight that neither swerves nor crosses its bound, the direct opposite of both the source's double-seeing eye and rebellious limit-crossing.
Human sights do not encompass God while He encompasses every sight, setting a precise boundary between the watched eye and the watcher it cannot see.
A barrier before and behind encloses people and covers them so they cannot see; the source's eye-enclosure becomes here an external enclosure that defeats eyesight.
After everyone comes to the appointed place in 19:71, God saves the mindful and leaves wrongdoers kneeling, marking the moral boundary within the common route.
Israel is warned not to transgress in good provision lest divine anger descend; abundance can be received within bounds or turn into the blow by crossing them.
The command not to transgress in the balance gives ط غ ي a measured boundary rather than the old peoples' unchecked movement through the land.
أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَآءَ صَبًّا uses the section's pouring root for life-giving rain, reversing the poured scourge while preserving the downward act.
Travelers are told to journey through closely spaced settlements by night or day in safety, the positive opposite of a road occupied by an ambusher.
The ark sails under God's eyes as recompense for Noah, showing the same divine watch as protective passage rather than capture.
The messenger is told to wait patiently for the Lord's judgment because he is under God's eyes, making the watched position one of care while the decree ripens.
Successive angels before and behind a person guard him by God's command; their stationed placement resembles 72:27 but functions as protection until a people change themselves.
The jinn find heaven filled with strong guards and flames; this supplies the guarded terrain in which 72:9's waiting flame catches the seeker.
The guards of 72:27 serve a knowledge-and-accounting purpose: God encompasses what is with the messengers and counts everything, clarifying the watch rather than merely its position.
Two receivers sit on the right and left to take each deed, establishing the fixed observation-post specified as a ready watcher in 50:18.
Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, moving the continually watched traveler into the judgment scene whose unveiled sight appears in 50:22.
God sends guardians over people until death and His messengers take the soul without neglect, a temporal watch that ends in the unavoidable encounter.
إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيْكُمْ رَقِيبًا states God's enduring watch over human relations, sharing the section's observer stance without the road setting.
Jesus says that after God took him, God alone was the watcher over his people, locating complete observation with the divine speaker.
God is watcher over every thing, extending the road-side image into universal surveillance.
No recitation or deed is entered without God being witness as people engage in it, and no smallest thing escapes Him; the watcher is present before actors notice an outcome.
Hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned, turning the faculties that failed ʿĀd into accountable witnesses.
Secret and private speech is heard while messengers beside the speakers record it, closely paralleling the ready watcher over every utterance in 50:18.
At the Fire, hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners, so the person's own faculties become the watching evidence.
The sinners could not hide from their own hearing, eyes, and skins; 41:20 identifies these organs as the witnesses they failed to anticipate.
Their false opinion about God's knowledge ruins them, showing inward judgment corrected by the watcher and bodily testimony in 41:20-22.
People have hearts with which they do not understand and eyes with which they do not see, directly distinguishing possession of the eye from the insight demanded by the section.
Insights have come from the Lord; whoever sees does so for himself and whoever remains blind bears that loss, articulating the inward meaning of the observer command.
The signs are within people's own selves and the ayah asks أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ, an explicit inward turn of the seeing eye.
Signs shown in the horizons and within people culminate in the Lord's witnessing of everything, moving from outer scene to inner recognition and then to divine watch.
The encounter of two armies is an عِبْرَةً for people of sight, showing a witnessed historical scene becoming inward lesson rather than visual report alone.
The stories of the former peoples contain an عِبْرَةً for those with understanding, supporting the source's dictionary sense of مَثَل as a lesson drawn from what is narrated.
The seizure of unjust towns is a sign for one who fears the Hereafter, whose day is gathered and witnessed; observed past judgment points toward the universal watchpoint.
The hearer is ordered to travel through the land and look at the deniers' end, making travelers deliberate observers of earlier judgments.
“Travel through the land, then look” at the deniers' end repeats the section's movement from route to perceptive seeing.
The question asks whether people have traveled in the land and seen the outcome of those before them, joining history's visible traces to judgment.
After messengers confront every nation, people are told to travel and see the deniers' end, a direct route from transgression to observed consequence.
The command to travel through the land and observe the criminals' outcome makes the listener a mobile witness of divine action.
Those who fail to travel and see the stronger former peoples' end repeat the blindness of ʿĀd despite visible cultivation and ruins.
Travel and look at the earlier people's end is again commanded, with their associationism naming the moral reading of the remains.
Travel should reveal the end of peoples stronger than the audience, showing that power cannot carry a traveler past God's grasp.
Travel through the earth would reveal how God seized peoples mightier and more marked in the land, closely echoing the observed ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh.
Former peoples' greater numbers, force, and آثار did not avail them; their remains are meant to be seen by later travelers.
The command to travel and see the old peoples' end says God destroyed them and promises the deniers comparable outcomes, making ruins an active warning.
Abraham asks his people about هَٰذِهِ ٱلتَّمَاثِيلُ; these literal statues instantiate the source dictionary's م ث ل form-word, distinct from its lesson sense.
The jinn make تَمَٰثِيلَ for Solomon, another concrete Quranic use of the source dictionary's “timsāl, an image,” without the idolatrous stance of 21:52.
Examples are set forth for each rejecting people before each is destroyed utterly, binding م ث ل to the observed consequences of collective transgression.
God sets forth examples for humankind, but only those with knowledge understand them; the source's “parable as lesson” depends on inward perception.
God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in the nearer life although it is slight beside the Hereafter; this identifies the valuation behind the false honor reading.
God expands and restricts provision and knows all things, separating measured livelihood from the person's estimate of his own standing.
The repeated expansion and restriction of provision belongs to the Lord, while spending is replaced by Him; both states remain acts of provision rather than verdicts on worth.
The question whether people know that God expands and restricts provision calls those changes signs, not independent proofs of honor or abasement.
The keys of heaven and earth belong to God, who expands and restricts provision; the two conditions proceed from one sovereign measure.
Qārūn emerges in adornment and observers longing for worldly life call his share mighty fortune, staging the first, wealth-centered look later corrected in 28:82.
Those given knowledge answer the dazzled observers that God's reward is better, supplying insight before Qārūn's visible collapse.
Qārūn and his house are swallowed by the earth with no rescuing faction; the sudden blow produces the changed sight confessed in 28:82.
Ruined towns, fallen roofs, abandoned wells, and lofty palaces supply the visible objects travelers should read with their hearts in 22:46.
The road-side ruins in 15:76 are declared a sign for believers, stating what the observer is meant to gain from the scene.
The overturned town receives layered stones rained down from above, a close nonlexical parallel to the scourge poured onto transgressors.
After the destructive rain, the hearer is told to look at the criminals' outcome, joining the descending blow to instructed observation.
An evil rain falls upon Lot's people, another punishment descending on those who had crossed their moral limit.
The rain upon Lot's people is called evil for those already warned, emphasizing that the blow arrives after notice yet still overtakes them.
God can send punishment from above or beneath the feet, giving the section's overhead pounce a wider statement of inescapable directions.
People are asked whether they feel secure from a storm of stones sent by the One above; its arrival would disclose the warning they ignored.
Thamūd are destroyed by ٱلطَّاغِيَةِ, a calamity named with the ط غ ي root's overwhelming excess and placed beside ʿĀd's visible end.
God destroys the former ʿĀd, directly naming the people whose fate the section tells the listener to see.
Noah's people are called more unjust and أَطْغَىٰ, repeating limit-crossing as the diagnosis of another destroyed people.
ʿĀd act arrogantly in the land and imagine no one stronger, a self-estimate that explains both their transgression and their failure to see the watcher.
Thamūd carve secure houses from mountains, a close counterpart to their cutting rock in the valley and confidence in works along the land.
The blast takes those supposedly secure rock-carvers at morning, turning their built route and refuge into the point of capture.
What Thamūd earned avails them nothing, completing the observed reversal of apparent security in 15:82-83.
God gives the fashioned human hearing, sight, and hearts, yet people give little thanks; the faculties exist before their inward use succeeds.
The Creator produces people and grants hearing, eyes, and hearts, but little gratitude follows, echoing the unused capacities of ʿĀd.
People emerge from the womb knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts so they may give thanks, stating the intended use of the eye's gift.
God originates hearing, sights, and hearts, yet little thanks is given, another boundary between being equipped to see and actually responding.
إِرْصَادًا describes a mosque established as an outpost for an enemy of God and His messenger, a different ر ص د use that still turns a fixed place into hostile waiting.
A barrier and حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا keep two bodies of water apart, giving the source's h-j-r eye-enclosure a Quranic boundary scene on a larger scale.

The punished Sabbath-breakers are made a warning example for contemporaries and later people; this plausibly supports the source's م ث ل-as-lesson strand, though the ayah uses نَكَٰلًا rather than the named root.
